note: Food as missions rather than listings. Each mission is a small assignment with candidates, what to order, and where to go afterwards. Moods map to missions in js/app.js.

items.title: Find Your Croissant
items.area: Three bakeries, all within a 15-minute walk of each other
items.priceNote: ~€12 for the whole thing, for two
items.brief: Everyone has a favourite croissant and almost nobody has actually compared them. Buy one plain croissant at each of the first three — plain, not almond, or the test means nothing — and eat them within an hour.
items.test: Judge on three things: does it shatter when you tear it, is the inside honeycombed rather than bready, and does it taste of butter after you swallow.

candidates.name: Du Pain et des Idées
candidates.order: Croissant + the pistachio-chocolate escargot
candidates.note: The benchmark. Closed weekends — this is a weekday mission.

candidates.name: Boulangerie Utopie
candidates.order: Plain croissant, then whatever is strange that week
candidates.note: The experimental one. Squid-ink baguettes, matcha everything.

candidates.name: Mamiche
candidates.order: Croissant, and a chocolate babka for later
candidates.note: Loud, cheerful, the opposite of hushed pâtisserie reverence.

candidates.name: Gonflé
candidates.order: Charcoal croissant with vanilla cream, and the kouign-amann
candidates.note: Ex-Plaza Athénée pastry chef, on a quiet street behind Gare du Nord.

then.text: Coffee at Ten Belles to reset your palate
Eat the winner on a bench in Jardin Villemin

items.why: The most useful hour you will spend on French food. By the end you will know which bakery is yours, which is a genuinely different thing from knowing which bakery is best.

items.title: The Baguette Test
items.brief: Ask for a baguette de tradition, not a baguette ordinaire — different flour rules, no additives, and about thirty cents more. Buy two from different bakeries on the same morning.
items.test: A good one has an irregular open crumb, a crust that crackles audibly as it cools, and a slightly cream-coloured interior rather than white. It should be noticeably better at 11:00 than at 17:00.

candidates.name: Du Pain et des Idées
candidates.order: Pain des amis — technically not a baguette, and better than one
candidates.note: Weekdays only.

candidates.name: Liberté, rue des Vinaigriers
candidates.order: Baguette de tradition
candidates.note: Open bakery — you watch them shape it.

candidates.name: Your nearest boulangerie
candidates.order: Baguette de tradition
candidates.note: The point of the test: the ordinary one near you might win.

then.text: Cheese from Marché Saint-Quentin to eat it with
A bottle from Le Verre Volé, six minutes away

items.why: Paris runs an annual competition for the best baguette in the city and the winner supplies the Élysée for a year. This is the same test, done by you, in one morning, for five euros.

items.title: Saturday Coffee Crawl
items.area: Three cafés, one neighbourhood, two hours
items.brief: Three stops, in order, no more than one drink each. Specialty first while your palate is clean, food in the middle, beautiful last.
items.test: Order the same thing at each — a flat white or a filter — so you are comparing the roast rather than the barista's latte art.

candidates.name: Café Oberkampf
candidates.order: Filter coffee and the shakshuka if you are hungry
candidates.note: Start here. Small, sunny, vegetarian-friendly.

candidates.name: Boulangerie Utopie
candidates.order: Whatever is seasonal and strange
candidates.note: The pastry stop, three minutes away.

candidates.name: Boot Café
candidates.order: Espresso, standing up
candidates.note: A former cobbler's the size of a shed. Three seats.

then.text: Ofr. for art books and magazines
Empreintes — four floors of French craft, free

items.why: Paris took a decade longer than London to take coffee seriously and then did it properly. This is the two-hour version of that story, walked rather than read.

items.title: Buy Cheese Like You Mean It
items.area: Marché Saint-Quentin, then anywhere with a view
items.brief: Go to a fromager, not a supermarket, and say: trois fromages, un doux, un fort, un de chèvre — s'il vous plaît. Then let them choose. Ask for it à point, meaning ready to eat today.
items.test: They will ask when you plan to eat it. That question is the whole difference between a cheese shop and a shelf.

candidates.name: Marché Saint-Quentin
candidates.order: Comté aged 24 months, a Saint-Nectaire, a small crottin
candidates.note: Your own 1866 iron market hall. Ten minutes away.

candidates.name: Marché d'Aligre
candidates.order: Whatever the counter is proudest of that week
candidates.note: The better market if you are making a morning of it.

candidates.name: Le Verre Volé
candidates.order: A bottle to go with it, at shop price
candidates.note: Six minutes from home, and they will match the wine to the cheese.

then.text: Baguette de tradition on the way home
Buttes-Chaumont, if the weather is behaving

items.why: France has something like 1,200 cheeses and most people living here rotate through four. One conversation with a fromager fixes that permanently.

items.title: Order a Bread You Cannot Pronounce
items.brief: Walk in and buy the thing on the shelf you have never bought. Then look it up afterwards rather than before.
items.test: A short list worth working through, none of which is a baguette.

candidates.name: Pain aux céréales / pain de seigle
candidates.order: Ask for it coupé — sliced
candidates.note: Rye and multigrain. The bread the French actually eat with oysters.

candidates.name: Fougasse
candidates.order: Fougasse aux olives
candidates.note: Flat, leaf-shaped, from Provence. Lunch on its own.

candidates.name: Pain aux noix or pain aux figues
candidates.order: A small one — it is dense
candidates.note: Walnut or fig bread. Made for a cheese board.

candidates.name: Chouquette
candidates.order: Ask for a hundred grams
candidates.note: Choux puffs with pearl sugar, sold by weight, absurdly cheap. The thing French children are given after school.

then.text: The cheese mission pairs directly with this
Coffee at Ten Belles to sit down with it

items.why: Living somewhere and understanding it are different, and the gap is usually made of small things you never got round to asking about. This one costs three euros to close.

items.title: Eat Your Way Through the 11th
items.brief: One arrondissement, six stops, from morning coffee to a glass of wine. The 11th has the best eating in Paris right now and it is twelve minutes from your door.
items.test: Do it in order and do not skip the cheese shop because you are full. That is the point of the walking between.

candidates.name: Café Oberkampf
candidates.order: Shakshuka and a filter
candidates.note: 09:30. Get there before the queue.

candidates.name: Boulangerie Utopie
candidates.order: Something you cannot identify

candidates.name: La Buvette
candidates.order: Beans in olive oil, and whatever cheese is out
candidates.note: 13:00. Fifteen seats in a former dairy.

candidates.name: Rue Paul Bert
candidates.order: Book one of the four bistros on the street
candidates.note: 20:00. Four good ones within thirty metres.

then.text: La Maroquinerie if there is a gig on
Moonshiner, through the pizzeria fridge door

items.why: This is how you stop being someone who lives in Paris and becomes someone who lives in a neighbourhood. Pick the 11th first because it rewards it fastest.

items.title: One Perfect Saturday — Canal Saint-Martin
items.brief: The whole day, on your doorstep, in order. Nothing here needs a Metro ticket.
items.test: The discipline is doing it in sequence and not going home in between. That is what turns errands into a day out.

schedule.text: Coffee at Ten Belles, taken outside to the water
Babka and a croissant from Mamiche
Walk the canal north through the locks
La Trésorerie and Artazart for the flat
Lunch in Passage Brady, under the glass roof
Bassin de la Villette — swim, kayak, or do nothing
Le Verre Volé, and buy a bottle to take home
Whatever is on at New Morning, nine minutes away

items.why: Most people who live somewhere good never do the thing visitors do — spend a whole day on it deliberately. This is that day, and it starts at the end of your street.
